title: Up, Down, Up Again
statement:
You get an integer array nums. It has an up-down-up shape if you can pick two indices p and q with 0 < p < q < n − 1 such that:

  • nums[0..p] is strictly increasing,
  • nums[p..q] is strictly decreasing,
  • nums[q..n − 1] is strictly increasing.

Each part has at least two values, and neighbouring parts share their turning point. Equal neighbours break every part, because "strictly" rules out flat steps. Return true if the array has this shape.

examples.why: Up 1 → 4 → 6, down 6 → 2, up 2 → 5. So p = 2 and q = 3.
The array must start by going up, and this one starts by going down.
The flat step 3 → 3 is neither strictly up nor strictly down.

hints: The shape is three monotonic runs in a row. How would you walk over the first run?
Move an index forward while the next value is bigger. Where it stops is p. Then keep moving while the next value is smaller; that stop is q.
Then walk up once more. The shape holds if p > 0, q > p, q < n − 1, and the last walk reaches the end of the array.

explain.intuition:
You do not need to try every pair (p, q). The turning points are forced: p must be the end of the longest strictly increasing run from the start, because the decreasing part cannot begin while values are still rising. Likewise q is where the decreasing run from p stops.

So walk one index through the array in three phases: up, down, up. After each phase check that it actually moved, which is what "each part has at least two values" means. If the third phase ends exactly at the last index, the shape is there. A flat step stops whichever phase is running, and the next phase cannot start on it either, so it fails naturally.
steps: Set i = 0. While i + 1 < n and nums[i] < nums[i + 1], move i forward. If i === 0, return false.
Let p = i. While i + 1 < n and nums[i] > nums[i + 1], move forward. If i === p or i === n − 1, return false.
Let q = i. While i + 1 < n and nums[i] < nums[i + 1], move forward. If i === q, return false.
pitfalls: Allowing an empty phase, so a plain up-down array like [1, 2, 1] passes. The last part needs at least two values.
Using ≤ or ≥ in the walks. Flat steps must break the shape.
Not checking that the final rise reaches the end. [1, 2, 1, 2, 1] goes up, down, up and then down again.

solutions.title: Try every pair of turning points
solutions.idea: For each p and q, check the three runs directly.

solutions.title: One walk in three phases
solutions.idea: The turning points are forced. Walk up, down, up, and check that each phase moved and the last one reaches the end.

followups: Find the contiguous subarray with this shape that has the largest sum.
Generalize: check whether the array splits into exactly k alternating strictly monotonic runs, starting with a rise.
